title: Genuinely multipartite entangled qudits: one rule to link them all
abstract: Links of rings offer an intuitive picture of multipartite entanglement. Cutting one ring can free some of the others, just as losing a particle, i.e. tracing it out, can disentangle some of the remaining ones. This analogy classifies multipartite entanglement according to which groups of particles stay entangled when others are lost, a question at the heart of robust quantum networks. However, pure states realizing a given link class were known only in special cases. Here, we close this gap. Recasting link polynomials as hypergraphs, we give an explicit formula for pure qudit states and prove that, for every link class, their entanglement under any pattern of particle loss matches the link exactly. The same construction also controls genuine multipartite entanglement, determining exactly which of the groups that stay entangled are genuinely multipartite entangled, and all of them can be made so. As a consequence, we prove the conjecture that $m$-resistant pure qudit states, which stay entangled after the loss of any $m$ particles but become fully separable after the loss of $m+1$, exist for any number of particles and any $m$.
summary: This paper establishes a deep connection between the topology of linked rings and the entanglement structure of qudit quantum states. By recasting link polynomials into hypergraphs, the authors derive explicit formulas for states that realize any desired entanglement pattern upon particle loss. This work proves the existence of highly robust, $m$-resistant entangled states, advancing the theory of quantum network resource quantification.
main_problem: To provide an explicit construction for pure qudit states that realize any given pattern of multipartite entanglement defined by link classes, and to characterize which entangled subsets are genuinely multipartite entangled.
main_result: The authors provide an explicit formula for pure qudit states corresponding to any link class, proving that the entanglement pattern (linked subsets vs. GME subsets) is precisely controlled by the underlying hypergraph structure.
method: The core method involves recasting link polynomials into hypergraphs and constructing the quantum state as a superposition over the hyperedges of this graph structure.
model_or_system: The system is multipartite entanglement in qudits, modeled using an analogy to linked rings. The entanglement structure is mathematically encoded by a hypergraph derived from the link polynomial.
key_observables: Link class (defined by polynomial), entanglement pattern upon particle loss, and the degree of genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) for reduced density matrices $\rho_S$.
important_parameters: The number of particles ($N$), the resistance level ($m$), and the structure of the hypergraph $g=(V,E)$.
main_assumptions: The construction assumes that the local dimension of the qudits is large enough to support the necessary superposition structure for all hyperedges.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mapping between link classes (e.g., Hopf link) and their corresponding hypergraphs, showing how the structure dictates entanglement properties.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the link between link polynomials and hypergraphs, then constructs the state $|\mathbf{g}\rangle$ based on this hypergraph. It proves two key theorems: one linking entanglement to graph connectivity, and another linking GME to the hyperedges themselves. Finally, it applies this to prove the existence of $m$-resistant states.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, concrete mathematical framework connecting topological invariants (link theory) directly to fundamental quantum resource properties (multipartite entanglement), which is highly relevant for designing robust quantum communication protocols.
